body: Russian licence plates are fully white with black text, lacking the blue strip common in the rest of Europe.
The Russian language uses the Cyrillic script and contains the special letters Ы, Э, Ё, and Ъ.
The Russian word for street is улица (ulitsa), which is different from the Ukrainian word вулиця (vulytsya).
The Russian word for city is город (gorod), abbreviated as г., while the Ukrainian word is місто (misto).
Russia has three main bollard types: a thin one on a stick, one with a black top and red reflector, and a German-style one.
Russia is known for having a large number of bollards near intersections.
Russian intersections are often unusually wide and feature many bollards.
Signposts in Russia often have black painted bottoms, a feature also common in Kazakhstan.
Russian utility poles often have concrete support blocks at the bottom, sometimes raising wooden poles off the ground.
Russian pedestrian signs show a person and three stripes, often with a bright yellow border. This design is shared with several other countries.
Russian pedestrian crossings have alternating white and yellow stripes, a feature also seen in Kazakhstan.
Black and white striped guardrails, kerbs, and bridge barriers are a common sight in Russia.
Russia commonly has Generation 3 coverage with a black or white car with a long antenna, or a short antenna with no visible car.
Urban housing in Russia is dominated by large, rectangular concrete apartment blocks.
Rural Russian houses are typically basic wooden structures with metal roofs.
Traditional Russian homes, especially log cabins, often feature richly decorated window frames, which are frequently painted blue.
Black & white-striped pole shields are common along highways, especially in European Russia.
Birch trees, with their white peeling bark, are widespread in Russia but are less common in the far south or far north of the European part.
Dense clusters of birch trees or forests composed solely of birches are a strong indicator for being east of the Urals.
Siberian larches, with their needle-like leaves, are a dominant tree in eastern Russia and at high elevations, becoming more common the further east you go.
Giant butterbur, or Sakhalin cabbage, is a very common plant in the southern half of Sakhalin Oblast.
The large white flower, Sosnowsky's hogweed, is most common around Moscow, the Komi Republic, and Perm Krai.
The pink or red flower fireweed is a strong indicator for the northern regions of Russia, and is common in most places north of Moscow.
Sunflower fields are common along the Ukrainian border and in more eastern oblasts like Ulyanovsk, Samara, and northern Orenburg.
Blue-pod lupines are very common in a specific area covering parts of Vladimir, Ivanovo, and Kostroma Oblasts.
The black poplar tree is common in southern Russia, near the borders with Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
The Russian olive tree is typically found along the Kazakhstan border.
Lined oak trees, often with a single white stripe on the trunk, are extremely common in Kaliningrad.
Sparsely planted larches along roads in open, rolling fields are a common landscape in Tatarstan and nearby regions.
Sandy roadsides are common in several regions, including Khanty-Mansi, Yamalo-Nenets, around Nizhny Novgorod, Karelia, Murmansk, and western Sakha.
Red soil is common in several areas, including around Izhevsk and Perm, Arkhangelsk, Leningrad, and Pskov Oblasts, and near Volgograd and Astrakhan.
The Kamchatka peninsula is characterized by unique grey gravelly soil and the largest number of volcanoes in Russia.
Extremely gravelly and sometimes dark soil is found when approaching the mountains east of Yakutsk.
The region around Vladivostok has lush, diverse forests in a hilly landscape with overcast coverage from a white car with a long antenna.
The eastern Kolyma Highway to Magadan features tall, hazy hills and mountains, unpaved roads with dark gravelly soil.
Siberian larches, large mountains, and a mostly paved road indicate the main road south of Yakutsk. Generation 4 coverage with a white car appears north of Berkakit.
Very hazy coverage, often orange or white, is found east and south of Mirny, especially along the Vilyuy river.
The landscape in Buryatia is unique, featuring an open grassy landscape with shrubs and mountains, which is lusher near Lake Baikal.
A forest fire haze near Lake Gusinoye in Buryatia can be distinguished from similar haze near Mirny by the open, rolling landscape.
The main road in the Altai Republic features a black car with a long antenna driving north through the Altai Mountains, often with foggy or rainy coverage.
Dry steppe mountains with a long antenna usually indicates the Tuva Republic.
Russia's far north, or tundra, is recognizable by its relatively flat landscape and very low vegetation.
Omsk Oblast has recognizable summer Generation 4 coverage with green agricultural fields interrupted by isolated patches of birch forest.
The area west of the Caspian Sea, particularly Kalmykia, Astrakhan Oblast, and Dagestan, is extremely dry and flat.
Early spring Generation 4 coverage with grassy fields and bushy vegetation is typical for Dagestan, which can be either flat or mountainous.
The Caucasus mountain range is one of Russia's largest, and includes Mount Elbrus, the country's tallest peak.
Rocks along the road are extremely common in Karelia and Murmansk Oblast.
An open, hilly landscape with low shrubbery and fireweed usually indicates Murmansk; lower shrubbery suggests a more northerly location.
Russian area codes can help with location: 8xx codes are in the west, 3xx are central, and 4xx are in the east or around Moscow.
In Generation 3 coverage, you can sometimes see unblurred licence plates with a regional code on the right side.
Bus stops unique to specific regions include Krasnoyarsk Krai, Chuvashia, Tatarstan, and Mari El.
Japanese cars with right steering become more common eastward, especially around Novosibirsk.
Thin bollards attached to sticks are mainly found in eastern Russia, starting near Omsk, with thicker Russian bollards still common.
Black traffic sign bottoms are primarily in Stavropol, Chechnya, and western Dagestan, with rare uncolored exceptions in other southern regions.
Pedestrian sign clips are found in Leningrad and St. Petersburg, very rarely in Pskov or Novgorod.
Dashed outer road lines are common in Kursk Oblast, with exceptions in Tuva, Karelia, Primorsky Krai, and Khabarovsk Krai.
Concrete block roads are typical further north, especially in Komi, Nenets, and Yamalo-Nenets.
Alternating red and white poles are mainly in Ulyanovsk and Nizhny Novgorod regions.
Striped red and white poles mostly appear in Saransk and Mordovia.
Bilingual signs are used in republics with minority languages, e.g., Bashkortostan and Tatarstan.
Town names in both Cyrillic and Latin alphabets are common near the Baltic border and Moscow.
Brown tourist signs pointing to attractions are common in Moscow Oblast and neighboring regions.
White limestone brick buildings are characteristic of Dagestan and nearby regions.
Red brick buildings are mostly in the south, with notable exceptions in Magnitogorsk, Orsk, and Omsk.
Mosques are most common in areas with Muslim majorities, such as South Russia, Tatarstan, and Bashkortostan.
Historical buildings in Mari El often feature green roofs, red bricks with white stone details, and similar church styles.
This map shows coverage in Russia, with sparse eastern and northern coverage, check the website for the extent.
White cars with long antennas are common in southern Chelyabinsk, Novosibirsk snow coverage, and Far East in Amur. Kamchatka's silver car with a B antenna is an exception.
Short A-type antennas have the highest ridge on the right, seen around Kaluga, Orenburg, and Krasnodar.
Short B-type antennas have the highest ridge on the left and are most common near Nizhny Novgorod, Elista, Yekaterinburg, and Tyumen.
Rectangular B-type antennas are limited to Moscow Oblast, Kurgan Oblast, southwest Krasnodar.
Twisting C-type antennas are mainly in north and east of Moscow, with Rostov Oblast furthest south.
Blurred short antennas are mainly near Ufa, Stavropol, and Makhachkala.
Long A-type antennas are mostly in Leningrad Oblast, Karelia, and Vologda Oblast, usually confirmed by white car long antennas.
Long B-type antennas are in Yaroslav, Tula, near Tuva and Irkutsk, with CB and CA variants less covered.
Blurred long antennas are common in Sakhalin, far east roads, and Khanty-Mansi, with some in western Bryansk and Tula.
Leaning short antennas tilt left and are mostly found along St. Petersburg to Volgograd, with exceptions in Stavropol and Ufa.
A large red brake light is common in Kaliningrad, and sometimes in western Russia.
Autumn coverage with Generation 3 is in Kaliningrad, Bryansk, Tula, and Belgorod; Kaliningrad only in autumn.
Generation 4 coverage is extensive across the country, mostly absent in the Altai mountains and Far East. The dark red indicates regions with full Generation 4 coverage.
Winter Generation 4 is mostly in the south of Russia, from Ryazan to Kabardino-Balkaria and Dagestan, with seasonal differences.
Spring Generation 4 appears around Kemerovo, Krasnoyarsk, Orenburg, Lipetsk, and Moscow, with landscape differences.
Summer Generation 4 is the most widespread, excluding south and east, with variations by car color.
Autumn Generation 4 is rare, mainly in Kazan, Murmansk, Ulan-Ude.
Generation 4 red cars are most common east of Khanty-Mansi, and along main highways to Irkutsk, Tatarstan, Rostov-on-Don.
White cars with generation 4 coverage are widespread around Lipetsk, Moscow, Sakha Republic, Magadan.
Generation 4 black cars are mostly found near Moscow, Tver, Voronezh, with some presence in Tatarstan and the south.
Vorkuta in far northern Komi shows dead-looking winter landscapes with reddish soil and large northern apartment block foundations.
Sovetskaya Gavan and Vanino have winter coverage like Vorkuta, though Vorkuta is flatter with lower vegetation.
The road to Okha in northern Sakhalin is unpaved with sandy soil and surrounded by short, stunted bushes and trees.
The Khabarovsk-Vanino road features mountainous landscapes and sunny coverage, with a black car having a blurred, long antenna.
The Jewish Autonomous Oblast has limited coverage with one main road; west side is rainy and foggy.
In the east of the Jewish Autonomous Oblast, coverage changes from rainy to wet.
P-297 in Amur Oblast has sunset coverage with the sun near the horizon and eastern-looking landscapes.
Olkhon Island has a single road on rolling sandy hills with sunset views of Lake Baikal and a mountain ridge.
Tunkinsky National Park in western Buryatia is a green river basin with tall jagged mountains to the north.
Northern Dagestan and southwestern Astrakhan Oblast have flat, desert-like Generation 4 coverage on small, poorly maintained dirt roads.
Tropical plants like palm trees in Russia occur only along the Black Sea, mostly near Sochi.
Kamchatka trekkers represent most Russian trekkers and are identified by typical Kamchatka clues.
Moscow has unique blue signs featuring English translations of tourist spots.
St. Petersburg street signs include a transliteration on a black background, mainly found downtown.
Saransk features circular street signs with street names in up to four languages.
Tatar bilingual signs use an abbreviated form for 'street' and are found in Tatarstan.
Bashkir bilingual signs appear in Bashkortostan, using the same word for 'street' as Tatar but often not abbreviated.
Chuvash bilingual signs use a distinct word for 'street' and are in Chuvashia.
Mari bilingual signs are found in Mari El, with their own term for 'street'.
Komi bilingual signs appear in Komi Republic, using a unique term for 'street'.
Yellow pole plates attached by metal bands are common in Tatarstan on most poles.
Many signposts on Murmansk’s main road and some in Karelia have two yellow bands wrapped around them.
Cobblestone pavements are common in Kaliningrad, Nizhny Tagil, Sverdlovsk, and Kizel.
Extended insulator bars on poles are common in southern Chelyabinsk, eastern Orenburg, and southern Kemerovo.
Utility poles with mesh frameworks are typical in Petrozavodsk and more rarely in cities like Tolyatti.
Red painted poles are exclusive to Murom.
Angled extended insulator bars on poles are characteristic of Chita.
A unique grey bollard with double red reflectors is found on the P100 in Kostroma Oblast.
Pedestrian signs with U-shaped hooks are unique to Chelyabinsk.
Distinct decorative pedestrian sign holders are specific to Pskov Oblast.
Nizhnevartovsk has unique hanging pedestrian signs.
Rounded rectangular fences with a line through the middle are unique to Chelyabinsk and eastern Orenburg Oblasts.
Fences with thin rounded rectangular tops appear in Syzran, Tolyatti, and Samara, often painted yellow in Tolyatti.
Bright orange decorative fences are unique to Irkutsk.
